subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I'm planning the hedgehog model's realistic proportions—about 20-25 cm long and 12 cm at shoulder height, facing +Z and standing at y=0—before writing the TypeScript builder code using the SDK's creation API.

Reviewing the SDK's methods for joints, chains, sweeps, rods, capsules, lofts, parts, surfaces, and membranes so I can structure the hedgehog's body, spines, and limbs correctly.

I'm also noting texture and shading helpers like paint, spots, stripes, mottle, and gradient for the skin, plus utility functions like rng, frame, and limb for procedural posing.

For required exports, I need a meta object with name and description, plus a default export function. I'm weighing whether to actually use the THREE import for something like geometry creation, since an unused import could be flagged by lint even though it's technically listed as required.

Now I'm designing a hedgehog puppet: a plump dome body with many cone-shaped spines in chestnut brown fading to cream tips. I'm working out how to color each spike's gradient from brown to cream based on its position along its length, since the built-in gradient function expects fixed points rather than per-spike coordinates — so I'm considering a custom paint function that uses the sweep's surface parameter to determine tip versus base coloring.

I'm also budgeting triangle counts: hundreds of individual spikes could push well past the 60k triangle limit, so I'm scaling down to around 140 spines with fewer sides and rings per spike to stay within budget while still looking convincingly spiky.

Each spike is swept individually, so meshes scale one-to-one with spine count, which I need to check against the part limit too. For direction, rather than having spines point purely along the surface normal, I want to bias them backward slightly to mimic a real hedgehog's lean, so I'm computing a blended direction vector combining normal and a tail-ward offset.

I also need to pull the base point slightly inward from the surface using the frame's local axes so the spine doesn't visually float, and I'm tracing through how weight inheritance works for the sweep path so the base point correctly picks up the surface hit's weights.

For scattering the spines, I'll use count and min-distance options with a filter to keep them off the face region and underside, limiting placement to the dome of the back where the normal points roughly upward.

As an alternative I'm considering a deterministic ring-based layout using azimuth/elevation ray-casting from the body center instead of random scatter, which would give more even control over spine density and avoid clustering near the face.

I need to keep the spines away from the face region at the front, using a distance filter from the head center to exclude that area from the belly too. Now I'm working out actual proportions: a plump body roughly 0.2m long with the head extending forward to a snout tip, building the overall shape as a loft along the z-axis for the dome-like body.

I'm defining the loft stations with widths and heights tapering at the ends for rounded caps, setting up rear, middle, and shoulder cross-sections before the neck tapers into the head, while keeping the back domed and the belly lower.

For the body proportions, I'm lowering the belly height and shortening the legs so a plump hedgehog shape sits properly with short legs and pink paws touching the floor, settling on center y around 0.085 with a half-height of 0.05 giving a believable overall body height.

Now I'm working out the loft station coordinates along the z-axis, starting with the rear taper point using width and height values for that section.

Rounding out the rest of the body stations — midsection widest around z=0, tapering toward the shoulders and neck at the front — then moving to the head shape, which I plan to build as a separate tapered loft running forward from the body base to a small pointed snout tip, picking station widths and heights that shrink down to a tiny rounded nose at the end.

I'm thinking about how the head and body meshes will overlap: since the head sits forward and slightly below body center, their surfaces will intersect near z~0.09-0.11, with the fawn-colored head effectively covering the body's front cap. Spines stay off the face region, so the overlap should look like a natural merge rather than a visible seam, as long as the head geometry fully conceals the body's front end.

I should place the head so it joins clearly beneath the spine dome, since the head bulges forward from the body's front-top, creating a face beneath the spines. Hedgehogs keep spines mostly behind the eyes with a bare forehead, so I'll filter spine placement to roughly z < 0.045 near the front, softening the boundary with a normal-based condition so spines still wrap the sides.

Now I'm working out the head's loft stations and how its radius shrinks toward the nose tip, checking that the base sits mostly inside the body volume so there's no visible seam. I'm also comparing the body's front cap radius against the head's radius at matching z-positions to make sure the body cap doesn't awkwardly poke out in front of the head.

Next I'm planning the facial features: a small black button nose sphere at the snout tip, and beady black eyes with tiny white highlight spheres placed on either side of the head using surface hit detection to find exact placement coordinates.

Now I'm figuring out the ears—small flattened spheres (scaled non-uniformly) placed near the sides of the head via stick-on-hit, positioning them roughly where the head surface curves outward near the eyes, with a slight embed so they sit naturally into the surface.

I'm untangling the orientation logic — a disc flattened along the outward normal lies flat against the head surface like a bump plate, but real ears stick out sideways with their broad face perpendicular to the surface, so I need the thin dimension oriented differently than I first assumed.

I'm checking that the stick scale maps to a flattened disc with the sphere's local Y as the outward normal, computing height from the scaled bounding box. For the eyes, I'm positioning small black spheres with white glint highlights on the sides of the head, aiming for that bright, beady look using the stick placement to orient them along the head's side normal.

Still working out glint placement...

For the nose, I'm placing a small flattened black sphere at the snout tip, slightly poking forward beyond the loft station there.

For twitchiness, I'm considering adding a few thin whisker rods extending from the snout sides in a dark brown color to give that alert, twitchy character detail.

Now I'm planning the leg structure: short pink-pawed legs attached to the belly, building out the skeleton starting with a root body joint and then adding a head joint.

For the legs, I'll use chains with two-point paths — hip to ankle — so each chain produces a leg bone and a tip "foot" joint, keeping front and hind legs consistent and simple to skin for the rig.

Then I'll sweep a mesh along each leg chain so the geometry bends naturally with the joints, tapering the radius slightly toward the paw, with brownish-fawn coloring for the limbs and pinkish tone for the paw pads.

For the paw itself, I'm placing a small flattened sphere scaled down vertically bound to the foot joint to form a pink pad, possibly with tiny toe bumps added for detail. I'm working out exact leg attachment heights relative to the belly and floor so the hip-to-paw span looks proportionate on the body.

For leg positions, I'm setting front legs near z=0.06 at x=±0.055 and back legs near z=-0.08 at x=±0.06, making sure the paws' lowest points touch or slightly sink into the floor. I'm deciding to build legs as proper skeletal chains with named hip and foot joints (like "hipFL" and "footFL") rather than plain rods, keeping joint names unique across the rig.

I'm also considering whether to give the legs a knee bend using a three-point path, but settling on straight stubby legs since hedgehogs have short limbs. Thinking about whether to add a jaw joint under the head for an openable mouth, following the general creature-rigging guidance that mouths should have separate upper and lower jaw parts.

I'm sketching a modest lower jaw piece as a small loft tucked beneath the snout, attached to a dedicated jaw joint positioned near the back of the head so it pivots convincingly. Working out loft station sizes...

Keeping it simple, I'll include the jaw joint and jaw mesh.

Now for the maple leaf stuck on the spines like a trophy: I'm weighing options between building an extruded polygon outline with multiple lobes versus using an SVG texture on a flat card with alpha cutout. The texture approach seems appealing since transparent pixels would cut the leaf shape away from the plane, but I'm uncertain whether SVG rasterization happens reliably given asynchronous texture loading.

Given the risk that the app might not wait for the texture to be ready, I'll go with a safer geometry-based approach: extruding a leaf outline with thin thickness and red coloring. I'm sketching out the classic five-lobed maple shape, placing lobe tips at specific angles around a central point with a small radius, plus sinus points between the lobes to carve out the characteristic notches.

Working out the coordinates...

Now I'm thinking about how to attach the leaf to the body — like a trophy skewered on spines, with a small dark stalk or spike piercing up from the back surface into the leaf's underside, tilting the leaf slightly for a natural impaled look.

Shifting the outline so the base sits at the origin, with the leaf extending upward to about 0.07 and lobes alternating out to roughly ±0.04 wide — that gives a maple-leaf shape around 8cm across, which is sizeable relative to the hedgehog's 20cm body but still believable as a trophy leaf.

I'm considering adding vein detail through a paint function keyed on local surface coordinates, darkening a central vein near x=0 and diagonal side veins, while keeping the extrude thin with a small bevel so the shape holds its sharp lobe tips and notches.

Now I'm checking texel density across the shared paint sheet: with total painted area (body, spines, head, legs) around 0.3 square meters, the texel density comes out to roughly 0.8mm per texel, which is just barely enough resolution for a 1.5mm leaf vein, so I need to be careful it doesn't get lost.

I'm also worried about chart packing — with 180 spines each potentially splitting into 6-12 charts by face direction, that's 1500-2000 tiny charts to pack into a 1024-wide sheet, and I need to verify the shelf-packing algorithm's padding and fill-ratio assumptions hold up before the height overflows the sheet.

For the spine shading itself, I'm defining a paint function that blends cream and brown based on position along the spine, giving a soft gradient near the tip rather than a hard boundary.

Now I'm planning the body and head colors: dark brown/black skin showing between spines, fawn tones for the head and legs, pink paws, and black eyes and nose. For ears I'm thinking fawn discs with a smaller pink inner disc to suggest the inner ear.

I'm now working out the spine placement and shape — scattering them across the dome but excluding the head and belly, orienting each spine to point outward along the surface normal with a slight backward lean, adding jitter, and setting small spike dimensions with a pointed tip and flat base using a low-poly cross-section.

I'm checking that triangle and part counts stay within budget: roughly 200 spines at a handful of rings each keeps triangle count in the tens of thousands and part count around 200, well under the limits.

I'm also sanity-checking visual density—whether 200 spines at the chosen minimum distance give adequate coverage across the body's surface area without looking sparse or overcrowded.

I'm checking that scatter's rejection sampling with a generous attempt budget still converges near the target count, and that the body sweep's meshes alone (excluding the head) are correctly passed as the surface target so buried-point checks work against only the body geometry.

I'm refining the scatter filters so spines stay off the face and belly while still covering the rump and sides, and working out the per-spine orientation logic so each spine leans outward and backward along its surface normal like a real hedgehog quill.

Checking types so the base point and direction inputs flow correctly through the spike-generation function, confirming the Spot frame carries the right joint weights for skinning, and dialing in spine length and radius variance for a natural, uneven look.

I'm tagging the spines with a "spine" group name for organization, then thinking about leaf placement — wanting it to look stuck onto the spines like a trophy. I'm working out which spine to pick near the back-top of the body, finding its tip point, and planning to anchor the leaf's base slightly below that tip so it appears pierced by the spine.

Still working out leaf orientation and plane directions...

I'm deciding to scale the leaf outline down by about 0.85 to keep proportions reasonable, and I'm about to rewrite the outline coordinates at that smaller scale.

I'm defining a single skewer spine that pierces up through the leaf's base to anchor it to the body, picking a hit point near the top of the body, a short length and slightly thicker radius than the scatter spines, and an upward-tilted direction, while considering whether one spine is enough versus using two for extra stability.

Simplifying it: skipping the inner disc entirely and just using a single pinkish-fawn color for the ears, flattened via a scaled sphere geometry so the ear sits thin against the head.
